# Introduction

## Fraud detection is a hard imbalanced-learning problem

Financial fraud detection is the task of flagging the small fraction of transactions, account openings, or transfers that are fraudulent within an overwhelming majority of legitimate activity. The defining property of the problem is extreme class imbalance: in the datasets studied in this thesis, fraud accounts for between roughly 0.13% and 1.5% of records (see @sec-datasets), and on the European credit-card benchmark only about 0.17% of transactions are fraudulent [@dalpozzolo2015calibrating]. Surveys of imbalanced learning have long noted that such skew breaks the assumptions of standard classifiers, which are biased toward the majority class when minimising aggregate error [@he2009learning_imbalanced_data].

A first consequence is that plain accuracy is meaningless as an evaluation metric. A trivial classifier that labels every transaction legitimate achieves over 99.8% accuracy on a 0.17%-fraud dataset while detecting nothing. Receiver-operating-characteristic (ROC) analysis is the standard remedy, but the ROC curve and its area can be optimistic under heavy skew because the false-positive axis is normalised by the large negative count [@fawcett2006roc_analysis]. This thesis therefore reports the area under the precision-recall curve (PR-AUC; equivalently, average precision) as its primary metric, since precision is sensitive to the positive base rate and rewards a classifier for ranking the rare fraud cases ahead of the legitimate ones [@davis2006relationship_pr_roc; @saito2015pr_more_informative_imbalanced].

A second consequence concerns the operating point. In practice an alert is reviewed at a cost, so a fraud detector is deployed at a fixed, low false-positive rate (FPR) rather than at an arbitrary 0.5 threshold. Accordingly, the secondary metrics are recall at 1% FPR and recall at 5% FPR: the fraction of fraud caught while incurring at most that many false alarms among legitimate transactions [@leborgne2022fraud_detection_handbook; @jesus2022baf_arxiv]. These metrics are computed conservatively from the empirical ROC curve, taking the highest achievable recall among thresholds whose FPR does not exceed the budget, rather than interpolating between curve vertices that do not correspond to any realisable threshold (this thesis's experiments; see @sec-methods). Classical responses to imbalance — resampling techniques such as SMOTE [@chawla2002smote] and loss reweighting such as focal loss [@lin2017_focal_loss] — all operate during training and require the model to be retrained for each objective.

## Gradient-boosted trees and the rise of tabular foundation models

For tabular prediction, gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDTs) remain the entrenched baseline. XGBoost [@chen2016xgboost_scalable_tree_boosting], CatBoost [@dorogush2018catboost], and LightGBM [@ke2017lightgbm] are routinely competitive with or superior to deep networks on heterogeneous tabular data, a robustness attributed to their handling of uninformative features and irregular target functions [@grinsztajn2022why_tree_based]. This thesis uses XGBoost and CatBoost, trained on the full training set, as its reference detectors.

A recent and disruptive alternative is the tabular foundation model (FTM). Building on the observation that large transformers [@vaswani2017attention_is_all_you_need] perform few-shot learning purely in-context — conditioning on examples supplied at inference time without any weight update [@brown2020language_models_few_shot] — Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) train a transformer on samples from a prior over datasets so that a single forward pass approximates Bayesian posterior-predictive inference [@muller2022transformers_bayesian_inference; @pfns_repo]. TabPFN applied this idea to tabular classification [@hollmann2023tabpfn; @hollmann2022tabpfn_arxiv], and TabPFN v2 was shown to match or beat tuned GBDTs on small and medium tables while requiring no per-dataset training [@hollmann2025accurate_tabular_foundation_model]. The family has since scaled and diversified — TabPFN 2.5 with a larger context window [@grinsztajn2025tabpfn25_arxiv; @priorlabs_tabpfn25_model_report_web], analyses of v2's behaviour [@ye2025closer_look_tabpfnv2], real-data continued pre-training [@garg2025real_tabpfn], scaling extensions [@liu2025tabpfn_unleashed], and the distinct TabICLv2 architecture [@qu2026tabiclv2]. FTMs already appear in financial applications [@olusegun2024ifs_tabpfn_ethereum; @priorlabs_taktile_case_study]. This thesis evaluates five FTMs: TabPFN v2, 2.5, 2.6, and v3, plus TabICLv2.

## The problem: a fixed context window wasted under imbalance

In-context learning (ICL) FTMs do not learn parameters from a training set; they read it as a sequence of in-context examples — the *context* — and process it through self-attention at inference. This context window is fixed and modest: roughly 10,000 rows for TabPFN v2 and 48,000–50,000 rows for the larger models in the grid (this thesis's experiments; see @sec-models). When the training set exceeds the window, it must be subsampled. The standard strategy is uniform random subsampling.

Under heavy class imbalance this strategy is wasteful. Sampling 10,000 rows at the natural 0.17% fraud rate yields, in expectation, only about 17 fraud examples; the remaining 9,983 slots are spent on legitimate transactions the model has already seen many of. Because the FTM forward pass is a posterior prediction conditioned on this context [@muller2022transformers_bayesian_inference], a context starved of the minority class can only produce a poorly informed posterior for that class. Moreover, what enters the context is itself a controllable inference-time lever — a property recently demonstrated adversarially for FTMs [@djilani2025robustness_tabular_foundation_models]. This thesis exploits the same lever for a benign, imbalance-motivated end. Two distinct deficiencies are at play: the context may be *irrelevant* (random rows are not structurally similar to the transactions being scored) and *imbalanced* (few fraud rows). RAP addresses both.

## The idea: Retrieval-Augmented Prediction

This thesis proposes **Retrieval-Augmented Prediction (RAP)**, a test-time context-construction strategy for ICL FTMs under heavy class imbalance. Rather than subsampling the context randomly, RAP constructs, per test batch, a context that is both structurally relevant and label-balanced. It proceeds in two steps. First, *retrieval*: for each batch of test rows, k-nearest-neighbour (kNN) retrieval in standardised feature space selects training rows similar to the batch, so the context is locally relevant to the transactions being scored. Second, *controlled fraud-ratio oversampling*: the retrieved pool is rebalanced to a target fraud ratio, supplementing scarce neighbourhood fraud from the global training-fraud pool and, when unique fraud is exhausted, duplicating fraud rows with replacement so that oversampling is the method rather than a silent cap (this thesis's experiments; see @sec-methods). The first step — relevance retrieval — is by now established for tabular models: TabR couples a deep network with kNN retrieval [@gorishniy2024tabr_nearest_neighbors], TabDPT bakes retrieval into a tabular foundation model [@ma2024tabdpt], and LoCalPFN retrieves a local neighbourhood for TabPFN [@thomas2024localpfn_retrieval_finetuning]. RAP's distinctive lever is the second step: deliberately *controlling the fraud ratio* of the retrieved context and sweeping it — an inference-time analogue of SMOTE-style oversampling [@chawla2002smote] that, unlike SMOTE, duplicates real transactions rather than synthesising them and requires no retraining of the frozen FTM. No prior retrieval-augmented tabular method tunes the in-context label composition for imbalance.

RAP is decomposed into an ablation that isolates each effect. A random-subsampling baseline (condition C1) is compared against retrieval at the natural fraud ratio (C3) to measure the *relevance* benefit — C3 is essentially the frozen kNN-context baseline already studied for TabPFN [@thomas2024localpfn_retrieval_finetuning] — and C3 against retrieval with ratio control (C4) to measure the *ratio-tuning* benefit, which is the thesis's novel lever. A stratified 50/50 subsampling condition (C2) isolates the ratio effect without retrieval.

## Contributions

This thesis makes the following contributions.

1. A clear articulation of why uniform random context subsampling is a poor fit for ICL FTMs under heavy class imbalance, framed through the posterior-predictive view of the FTM forward pass.
2. RAP, a test-time context-construction method for frozen ICL FTMs that augments relevance-based kNN retrieval — established for tabular ICL by TabR, TabDPT, and LoCalPFN [@gorishniy2024tabr_nearest_neighbors; @ma2024tabdpt; @thomas2024localpfn_retrieval_finetuning] — with *controlled, swept in-context fraud-ratio oversampling*, the component without precedent in that literature.
3. An empirical evaluation across five FTMs and two GBDT baselines on six public financial-fraud datasets, using prevalence-corrected PR-AUC and conservative recall-at-fixed-FPR metrics.
4. An ablation that decomposes RAP's benefit into a (largely confirmatory) relevance component and a (novel) ratio component, plus a sweep of the target fraud ratio — directly testing whether two results from adjacent settings hold under heavy tabular imbalance: that random context selection is a strong baseline [@feuer2023scaling_tabpfn] and that ratio rebalancing of in-context examples is ineffective [@gao2025imbalanced_annotations].

## Research questions

The evaluation is organised around four research questions (RQs), mapped to the experimental conditions described in @sec-methods.

- **RQ1 — FTMs versus GBDTs under random subsampling.** How do ICL FTMs, given a randomly subsampled context (C1), compare to GBDTs trained on the full dataset, measured by PR-AUC and recall at fixed FPR? This establishes the baseline in the specific fraud / prevalence-corrected-PR-AUC regime that prior FTM benchmarks (balanced, accuracy-oriented) do not cover.
- **RQ2 — Does random subsampling degrade at scale?** Does FTM detection under random subsampling (C1) deteriorate as dataset size grows, relative to the unconstrained GBDT baselines? This re-confirms, for the modern FTM line under fraud-scale imbalance, a context-scaling degradation already reported for TabPFN [@thomas2024localpfn_retrieval_finetuning; @ma2024tabdpt].
- **RQ3 — Does retrieval improve over random subsampling?** Does kNN-retrieved context (C3) improve PR-AUC over random subsampling (C1), isolating the relevance effect? This is largely *confirmatory*: a frozen kNN context already beats a random one for TabPFN [@thomas2024localpfn_retrieval_finetuning]. RQ3 re-tests that on modern FTMs under heavy imbalance, and against the competing finding that random context selection is a strong baseline that smart selection struggles to beat [@feuer2023scaling_tabpfn].
- **RQ4 — What is the optimal context fraud ratio?** Across the C4 sweep over target fraud ratios {5%, 10%, 20%, 30%, 50%}, which ratio maximises detection, and does ratio tuning add value beyond retrieval alone (C4 versus C3)? This is the thesis's **primary, novel** question: no retrieval-augmented tabular method controls the in-context label ratio, and an analogous result in language-model ICL found ratio rebalancing ineffective [@gao2025imbalanced_annotations], so the outcome is genuinely open.

RQ1–RQ3 establish and confirm the setting; RQ4 is the central contribution. The RAP conditions (C3 and C4) are implemented in the next phase of the project, so results for RQ3 and RQ4 are pending.

## Thesis outline

The remainder of the thesis is structured as follows. @sec-background reviews the necessary background: in-context learning, the PFN and TabPFN line of work, the GBDT baselines, and the class-imbalance and evaluation literature. @sec-datasets documents the six fraud-detection benchmarks, their provenance, and their split protocols, including the deliberately retained time features and the one synthetic dataset found to be degenerate. @sec-methods specifies the experimental methodology: the four context-construction conditions, the five FTMs and their context limits, the prevalence-corrected metrics, and the RAP pipeline design. The results chapter reports the four research questions in turn. The final chapters discuss limitations — including single-GPU tractability compromises and the questionable meaningfulness of distance-based retrieval over ordinal-encoded entity identifiers — and conclude.

# Background {#sec-background}

This chapter assembles the conceptual foundations the rest of the thesis builds on. It moves from the problem (supervised fraud detection under extreme class imbalance) through the model families involved (gradient-boosted decision trees, then in-context-learning tabular foundation models) to the precise structural limitation that Retrieval-Augmented Prediction (RAP) is designed to address: the fixed context window of an in-context-learning model and how random subsampling of that context starves it of the minority class. Every domain term and acronym is defined on first use.

## Supervised fraud detection under extreme class imbalance

Fraud detection is, in this thesis, a supervised binary classification problem. Each transaction (or account-opening application) is a feature vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ with a label $y \in \{0, 1\}$, where $y = 1$ denotes fraud (the *positive* or *minority* class) and $y = 0$ denotes a legitimate event (the *negative* or *majority* class). A model produces a score $s(x) \in [0, 1]$ interpreted as $\Pr(y = 1 \mid x)$, and a decision is taken by thresholding that score. The defining property of the setting is *extreme class imbalance*: the prevalence $\pi = \Pr(y = 1)$ is very small. Across the six benchmark datasets used in this thesis it ranges from roughly 0.13% to 1.5%, and in the most extreme case (the PaySim mobile-money dataset) it is about 0.13%; the European credit-card benchmark, at about 0.17%, has only around 98 fraudulent transactions in a held-out test set [@dalpozzolo2015calibrating]. Such skew breaks the naive baseline: a classifier that predicts "legitimate" for every input attains over 99% accuracy while detecting no fraud at all. Accuracy is therefore uninformative here, and the imbalanced-learning literature has long argued that both the learning algorithm and its evaluation must be adapted to the minority class [@he2009learning_imbalanced_data].

### Evaluation metrics

Because accuracy is degenerate under imbalance, this thesis evaluates models with threshold-free, rank-based metrics. The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve plots the true-positive rate (TPR, equivalently recall) against the false-positive rate (FPR) as the decision threshold is swept, and the area under it (ROC-AUC) summarises ranking quality independent of any single threshold [@fawcett2006roc_analysis]. ROC-AUC has a known weakness under heavy imbalance, however: because the FPR is normalised by the large pool of negatives, a model can move many false positives in absolute terms while barely perturbing the FPR, so ROC-AUC can look optimistic when the positive class is tiny [@fawcett2006roc_analysis]. The precision-recall (PR) curve instead plots precision against recall; precision depends directly on the absolute number of false positives relative to true positives, so the PR curve and the area under it (PR-AUC, equivalently average precision) are far more sensitive to minority-class performance and are the preferred summary under severe skew [@davis2006relationship_pr_roc; @saito2015pr_more_informative_imbalanced].

This thesis reports **PR-AUC** (average precision) as its primary metric, supplemented by two operating-point metrics, **Recall@1%FPR** and **Recall@5%FPR**, and by ROC-AUC and F1 as secondary diagnostics. The recall-at-fixed-FPR metrics reflect the operational reality of fraud screening, where an institution can only manually review a small, fixed fraction of flagged transactions and therefore fixes a low false-positive budget [@leborgne2022fraud_detection_handbook]. In this thesis's experiments these metrics use a deliberately conservative definition: Recall@$k$%FPR is the highest TPR among the operating points of the *empirical* ROC curve whose FPR is at most the target. Linear interpolation between empirical ROC vertices is avoided on purpose, because an interpolated (FPR, TPR) pair corresponds to no achievable decision threshold and thus overestimates attainable recall — an effect that is pronounced when the positive class is small and the ROC is coarse, as in the European credit-card dataset. The methods chapter returns to this and to the prevalence correction applied to PR-AUC under test-set subsampling.

### Classic imbalance remedies

The imbalanced-learning literature offers three broad families of remedy [@he2009learning_imbalanced_data]. *Data-level* methods rebalance the training distribution; the canonical example is SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique), which generates new minority examples by interpolating between a minority point and its nearest minority neighbours rather than merely duplicating rows [@chawla2002smote]. *Algorithm-level* or *cost-sensitive* methods leave the data alone but reweight the learning objective so that errors on the minority class are penalised more heavily; focal loss is a widely used instance that down-weights easy, well-classified majority examples and concentrates training on hard minority examples [@lin2017_focal_loss]. *Ensemble* and clustering approaches combine resampling with multiple learners. A recurring finding on these benchmarks is that, under extreme imbalance, the choice of training objective can matter more than the choice of architecture [@sun2025extreme_imbalance_baf].

These remedies share an assumption that the model is being *trained*: SMOTE alters the training set, focal loss alters the loss minimised during training, and cost weights enter gradient updates. That assumption does not hold for the in-context-learning models at the centre of this thesis, whose weights are frozen at inference time. RAP can be read as a data-level remedy relocated to inference: rather than resampling a training set before fitting, it constructs a relevant, label-balanced *context* at prediction time. The next sections build up to why such a model exists and why its context is the natural place to intervene.

## Tabular machine learning and gradient-boosted decision trees

Most fraud data is *tabular*: heterogeneous columns of numeric and categorical features, no spatial or sequential structure that convolutional or recurrent inductive biases would exploit. For two decades the dominant approach to tabular prediction has been the gradient-boosted decision tree (GBDT), an additive ensemble that fits each new shallow tree to the gradient of the loss left by the current ensemble. XGBoost provides a scalable, heavily regularised implementation that became a default strong baseline across tabular competitions and applications [@chen2016xgboost_scalable_tree_boosting]. CatBoost contributes ordered boosting (a permutation-driven scheme that mitigates target leakage) and native handling of categorical features, which is useful given that several fraud datasets carry categorical columns such as transaction type or device operating system [@dorogush2018catboost]. LightGBM rounds out the family with histogram-based splitting tuned for speed on large datasets [@ke2017lightgbm].

Deep learning was slow to displace GBDTs on tabular data. A careful empirical study attributes the gap to properties of tabular targets: they are often irregular, non-smooth functions of the inputs, they contain uninformative features that neural networks struggle to ignore, and they lack the locality or invariance structure that gives deep models their edge on images and text [@grinsztajn2022why_tree_based]. GBDTs, by contrast, are rotationally non-invariant axis-aligned learners that handle uninformative features and irregular boundaries gracefully. This robustness is exactly why this thesis treats XGBoost and CatBoost as strong baselines rather than as straw men. They are trained on the full training set with no context limit, because the limited context window is an inherent property of the foundation models being evaluated, not a constraint that should be imposed on the baselines. The central empirical question — whether context-aware in-context learning can close the gap to GBDTs under heavy imbalance — only has meaning against such well-tuned tree baselines.

## In-context learning and Prior-Data Fitted Networks

The foundation-model side of the thesis descends from the Transformer, an architecture that replaces recurrence with self-attention so that every element of an input set can attend to every other element in a single forward pass [@vaswani2017attention_is_all_you_need]. Self-attention is the substrate on which the tabular foundation models studied here operate: a row's prediction is computed by attending over a set of labelled rows supplied alongside it. A pivotal observation about large Transformer language models was that they perform *few-shot learning purely in-context* — given a handful of input-output examples in the prompt at inference time, they generalise to new inputs without any gradient update to their weights [@brown2020language_models_few_shot]. This is *in-context learning* (ICL): the examples conditioned upon, not the weights, carry the task-specific information.

Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) give ICL a Bayesian interpretation [@muller2022transformers_bayesian_inference]. A PFN is a Transformer trained on synthetic datasets drawn from a prior over data-generating mechanisms; its training objective makes it approximate the *posterior predictive distribution* — the probability of a query label given the conditioned examples, marginalised over the prior — in one forward pass. The expensive Bayesian inference is amortised into pre-training; at inference the network simply conditions on the supplied examples and reads off an approximate posterior. The open PFN training infrastructure that underlies this line of work is publicly maintained [@pfns_repo].

TabPFN applied PFNs to tabular classification [@hollmann2023tabpfn; @hollmann2022tabpfn_arxiv]. A single pre-trained Transformer takes a small labelled training table as in-context examples and classifies a query table in one forward pass, with no per-dataset training and no hyperparameter search. The original model targeted the small-data regime and carried a modest cap on the number of in-context rows it could ingest — the very constraint that, scaled up to heavily imbalanced data, RAP works within. The Bayesian framing is the lens through which the rest of this thesis reads the context: if the forward pass approximates a posterior predictive conditioned on the supplied examples, then *which* examples are supplied directly shapes the posterior, and a context that is both relevant to the query and adequately populated with the minority class should yield a sharper posterior under imbalance.

## Tabular foundation models

The TabPFN line has since matured into a family of *tabular foundation models* (FTMs) — pre-trained models intended to be applied off-the-shelf across many tabular tasks. TabPFN v2, published in *Nature*, scaled the prior, the architecture, and the supported data size, and reported matching or exceeding tuned GBDT baselines on small and medium tabular datasets while running in seconds and requiring no per-dataset tuning [@hollmann2025accurate_tabular_foundation_model]. Subsequent releases pushed capacity further: TabPFN 2.5 enlarged both the context capacity and accuracy over v2 [@grinsztajn2025tabpfn25_arxiv; @priorlabs_tabpfn25_model_report_web], and TabPFN 2.6 and v3 continued the series within the same model family [@priorlabs2026tabpfn26_model_card; @grinsztajn2026tabpfn3_technical_report]. A parallel architecture, TabICLv2, offers an alternative open ICL tabular model with a large context capacity, providing a useful test of whether context-construction effects generalise beyond the TabPFN family [@qu2026tabiclv2]. Active research extends FTMs along orthogonal axes — continued pre-training on real rather than purely synthetic data [@garg2025real_tabpfn], scalability and ensembling strategies [@liu2025tabpfn_unleashed], resilience to distribution drift [@helli2024drift_resilient_tabpfn], analyses of why TabPFN v2 works and where it fails [@ye2025closer_look_tabpfnv2], and training-free relational extensions [@xu2026rdb_foundation_model]. RAP is complementary to all of these: it improves the *test-time context* rather than the model weights or the prior.

Mechanically, an ICL FTM does classification by *conditioning on a training context at inference*. The model receives a context $(X_{\text{ctx}}, y_{\text{ctx}})$ of labelled rows together with the unlabelled query rows; a single forward pass attends across the context and emits class probabilities for the queries. There is no fitting in the GBDT sense — what the wrappers in this thesis call `fit` merely loads the context into the frozen model, and `predict_proba` performs the conditioned forward pass. Because the context is supplied at inference, it is a fully controllable lever: prior work has shown, in an adversarial setting, that perturbing the in-context set can steer FTM predictions, demonstrating that the context is a genuine attack surface and, equivalently, a genuine design surface [@djilani2025robustness_tabular_foundation_models]. FTMs are already entering tabular benchmarking leaderboards alongside the classical baselines [@tabarena_openreview], are surveyed within the broader arc of representation learning for tabular data [@jiang2026representation_learning_tabular_survey], and are appearing in applied financial settings, from Ethereum fraud detection [@olusegun2024ifs_tabpfn_ethereum] to an industrial financial-risk deployment [@priorlabs_taktile_case_study]. This thesis asks whether they can be made competitive fraud detectors specifically under heavy imbalance, and whether the lever for doing so is the context.

## The context-window bottleneck under imbalance

The crux of the thesis is a structural mismatch between how an ICL FTM consumes a context and what extreme imbalance does to a randomly drawn one. Each FTM supports only a bounded number of context rows. The models evaluated here, with their soft context limits (the upper end of their pre-training range, in rows), are summarised below; these limits are read from the model wrappers used in the experiments.

| Model | Context limit (rows) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| TabPFN v2 | 10,000 | smallest context in the grid |
| TabPFN 2.5 | 50,000 | enlarged context vs v2 |
| TabPFN 2.6 | 50,000 | same family capacity |
| TabPFN v3 | 50,000 | provisional, pending checkpoint confirmation |
| TabICLv2 | 48,000 | no hard cap; pre-training upper bound |

*Source: model wrappers in this thesis's codebase (`src/models/ftm.py`); context limits per [@hollmann2025accurate_tabular_foundation_model; @grinsztajn2025tabpfn25_arxiv; @qu2026tabiclv2].*

When the training set is larger than the context limit, the baseline strategy (condition C1 in this thesis) is to draw a uniform random subsample of the training rows up to the limit. Under heavy imbalance this subsample inherits the population prevalence in expectation, which is the problem. If the prevalence is $\pi$ and the context holds $c$ rows, the expected number of fraud rows in a uniform random context is $\pi c$. For TabPFN v2's 10,000-row context, a 0.13%-prevalence dataset such as PaySim [@lopezrojas2016_paysim] yields about 13 expected fraud rows, and a 0.17%-prevalence dataset such as the European credit-card benchmark [@dalpozzolo2015calibrating] yields about 17; at the larger 48,000–50,000-row contexts those counts rise only to roughly 62–65 and 82–85 respectively. The context window is therefore flooded with legitimate transactions while the minority class — the only class the task actually cares about — is represented by a handful of rows. The exact counts depend on dataset prevalence and the per-model limit; representative values are tabulated below.

| Dataset (prevalence) | Expected fraud rows @ 10k | @ 48k | @ 50k |
|---|---|---|---|
| PaySim (0.13%) | ~13 | ~62 | ~65 |
| eu_cc (0.17%) | ~17 | ~82 | ~85 |
| BAF (1.1%) | ~110 | ~528 | ~550 |
| BankSim (1.2%) | ~120 | ~576 | ~600 |

*Expected fraud count $= \pi c$ for a uniform random context of size $c$; prevalences per the dataset chapter of this thesis.*

This is the precise gap RAP targets. Two distinct deficiencies are at work, and the experiment design (detailed in the methods chapter) is structured to separate them. First, a uniform random context is *irrelevant* to a given query: it is a random slice of the whole training distribution rather than the region of feature space the query inhabits. RAP addresses this with k-nearest-neighbour (kNN) retrieval, building a context from the training rows nearest to each test batch. Second, even a relevant context inherits the population prevalence and so remains starved of fraud; RAP additionally rebalances the retrieved context to a controlled fraud ratio by oversampling minority rows. The first intervention echoes the few-shot insight that the supplied examples carry the task signal [@brown2020language_models_few_shot], applied at the granularity of the individual query; the second is a data-level imbalance remedy [@he2009learning_imbalanced_data] relocated from training time to inference time, conceptually adjacent to SMOTE-style oversampling [@chawla2002smote] but operating on the FTM's context rather than on a training set. Because the FTM forward pass approximates a posterior predictive conditioned on its context [@muller2022transformers_bayesian_inference], improving the relevance and class balance of that context is a principled way to sharpen the posterior under extreme imbalance — without retraining, reweighting, or altering the frozen model in any way.

The methodological building blocks RAP relies on are themselves standard. kNN retrieval over feature space, demonstration selection for in-context learning, and the choice of distance metric and feature scaling for that retrieval are established techniques [@liu2022good_in_context_examples; @rubin2022learning_to_retrieve_prompts; @cover1967nearest_neighbor_pattern_classification; @hastie2009elements_statistical_learning] whose specific instantiation in this thesis is deferred to the methods chapter. What matters for the present chapter is the framing: a frozen ICL tabular foundation model, evaluated under prevalence around 0.1–1%, with a fixed context window that random subsampling fills almost entirely with the majority class. RAP is the test-time strategy that fills that window differently.

# Related Work

This chapter positions Retrieval-Augmented Prediction (RAP) against four threads of prior work. The first traces the lineage of the TabPFN family of tabular foundation models (FTMs) and the parallel effort to scale their in-context-learning (ICL) capacity. The second surveys FTMs and transformers applied to fraud and finance. The third reviews classical and deep fraud detection together with the broader class-imbalance literature, including the anti-money-laundering (AML), graph, and synthetic-data work that surrounds it. The fourth frames RAP itself as retrieval-augmented ICL specialized to heavily imbalanced tabular data. Each thread closes with the gap it leaves, and those gaps jointly motivate the contribution of this thesis.

## The TabPFN lineage and the scaling of context

The line of work this thesis builds on begins with the observation that transformers [@vaswani2017attention_is_all_you_need] perform few-shot learning purely in context, conditioning on examples supplied at inference without any weight update [@brown2020language_models_few_shot]. Müller et al. [@muller2022transformers_bayesian_inference] recast this as approximate Bayesian inference: a Prior-Data Fitted Network (PFN), trained on samples drawn from a prior over datasets, approximates the posterior predictive distribution in a single forward pass. TabPFN ported the PFN recipe to tabular classification [@hollmann2023tabpfn; @hollmann2022tabpfn_arxiv], and TabPFN v2 demonstrated that a single pre-trained transformer matches or surpasses tuned gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDTs) on small and medium tables [@hollmann2025accurate_tabular_foundation_model]. The PFN training methodology and reference implementations are maintained in open repositories [@pfns_repo; @priorlabs_tabpfn_repo].

The family has since advanced along two axes. The first is the model itself: TabPFN-2.5 enlarges the usable context and improves accuracy over v2 [@grinsztajn2025tabpfn25_arxiv; @priorlabs_tabpfn25_model_report_web], analyses of v2 dissect why it works and where it fails [@ye2025closer_look_tabpfnv2], Real-TabPFN improves the prior by continued pre-training on real-world tables rather than purely synthetic ones [@garg2025real_tabpfn], and Drift-Resilient TabPFN extends ICL to temporal distribution shift [@helli2024drift_resilient_tabpfn]. TabICLv2 offers an alternative ICL architecture with a large, open context and faster inference [@qu2026tabiclv2]. A complementary direction widens the data substrate beyond single tables: a training-free relational-database foundation model argues that strong relational predictions need no bespoke pre-training [@xu2026rdb_foundation_model]. The benchmarking and survey backdrop — living tabular leaderboards [@tabarena_openreview] and a survey of representation learning for tabular data [@jiang2026representation_learning_tabular_survey] — frames where these models currently stand relative to the GBDT baselines [@grinsztajn2022why_tree_based; @chen2016xgboost_scalable_tree_boosting; @dorogush2018catboost; @ke2017lightgbm] this thesis also evaluates.

The second axis is scale, which is the one most relevant here. TabPFN Unleashed proposes scalability and effectiveness extensions, including context-handling and ensembling strategies, to push TabPFN toward larger problems [@liu2025tabpfn_unleashed]. The official extension tooling [@priorlabs_tabpfn_extensions] and the model-version progression measured in this thesis — TabPFN v2 at roughly a ten-thousand-row context window and TabPFN 2.5, 2.6, v3, and TabICLv2 at roughly forty-eight to fifty thousand rows [@tabarena_openreview; @grinsztajn2026tabpfn3_technical_report] — both treat the context as something to make *larger*. None of this work, however, treats the context as something to *compose*. The implicit assumption is that, given more capacity, a representative subsample of the training set suffices. Under heavy class imbalance that assumption breaks: a random subsample drawn at the natural fraud rate of roughly one in a thousand floods even a fifty-thousand-row window with legitimate transactions and may contain only a handful of fraud rows, or none. The gap this thread leaves is precise: no member of the TabPFN lineage addresses *test-time context construction under extreme imbalance*, where which rows enter the window matters more than how many it can hold.

## Foundation models and transformers in fraud and finance

A small but growing body of work applies FTMs and related transformers to financial-crime tasks, establishing both feasibility and the practical stakes of improving them. Olusegun et al. apply an explainable TabPFN-style tabular transformer to Ethereum fraud detection and report improved detection with interpretability, demonstrating that a frozen FTM is a viable fraud classifier [@olusegun2024ifs_tabpfn_ethereum]. On the industrial side, a Prior Labs case study describes deploying TabPFN for financial risk management in collaboration with Taktile [@priorlabs_taktile_case_study], and the vendor documents an unsupervised anomaly-detection mode for the same model [@priorlabs_docs_anomaly_detection]. Beyond single-model classification, a multi-agent debate framework has been proposed for tabular anomaly detection [@wang2026_multi_agent_debate_tabular_anomaly], signaling interest in composing FTMs into larger detection systems.

Two findings in this thread bear directly on the present design. First, the robustness study of Djilani et al. shows that the in-context set is a controllable test-time lever: adversarial manipulation of the supplied context degrades FTM predictions, and the proposed defenses also operate by editing the context [@djilani2025robustness_tabular_foundation_models]. This establishes, academically, that *what enters the context changes the prediction* — RAP is a benign, imbalance-motivated instance of the same mechanism. Second, the anomaly-detection framing [@priorlabs_docs_anomaly_detection] is unsupervised, whereas fraud detection here is supervised with scarce but informative labels. The gap this thread leaves is that existing FTM-for-fraud work either takes the context as given (single-model classification and case studies) or abandons supervision (anomaly detection); none deliberately *constructs* a supervised, label-balanced, relevance-targeted context to counteract imbalance, even though the robustness literature shows the context is exactly the right surface to act on.

## Classical and deep fraud detection and class imbalance

Fraud-detection research has largely pursued an architectural and objective-level arms race. Recent deep models include energy-based Restricted Boltzmann Machines combined with xLSTM for real-time card fraud [@baghdadi2025rbm_xlstm_fraud], DBSCAN-augmented disjunctive voting ensembles that use density-based clustering to separate the minority class [@ghalwash2025dbscan_dve_fraud], and deep networks paired with focal loss and resampling on the European card benchmark [@albalawi2025focal_loss_fraud]. Relational and structured systems take a different route: a three-level relationship-penetration support system uncovers coordinated fraud through entity structure [@li2024financial_fraud_support_system], and graph-database integration has been demonstrated on the BankSim payment simulator [@patil2024graphdb_banksim]. A closely related and instructive finding comes from Sun et al., who argue that under extreme imbalance on the Bank Account Fraud (BAF) suite the training objective matters more than the model architecture [@sun2025extreme_imbalance_baf]. That conclusion motivates the stance taken here: rather than add another architecture, RAP intervenes on what the model conditions on at inference.

A parallel strand addresses financial crime at the network level. Realistic synthetic transaction graphs have been generated for AML model development with controllable laundering typologies [@altman2023realistic_synthetic_aml]; graph-neural methods detect laundering on transaction graphs, including a multi-aggregation Graph Isomorphism Network [@wojcik2025magic_gin_aml] and temporal graph networks for time-evolving financial anomalies [@kim2024temporal_gnn_financial]; knowledge-based multi-agent frameworks both generate and detect laundering patterns [@huda2025amlnet_framework]; and federated learning has been used to detect mule accounts across institutions without sharing raw data [@okeke2025federated_mule_fraud]. Applied machine-learning studies on individual benchmarks, such as PaySim [@alumona2025paysim_ml], round out the conventional-baseline picture. This thesis deliberately operates in the purely tabular, single-table feature space and treats these graph, relational, and federated approaches as complementary rather than competing.

The imbalance methodology underpinning all of this is well established. Classical resampling synthesizes minority examples by interpolating between near neighbours (SMOTE) [@chawla2002smote]; objective-level methods reweight the loss to focus on hard minority examples (focal loss) [@lin2017_focal_loss]; and surveys catalogue the sampling, cost-sensitive, and algorithm-level families together with appropriate evaluation metrics [@he2009learning_imbalanced_data]. The evaluation protocol of this thesis follows the ROC and precision-recall tradition for skewed data, which warns against accuracy and naive thresholds [@fawcett2006roc_analysis] and motivates the use of PR-AUC (area under the precision-recall curve), Recall at fixed false-positive rate (FPR), and ROC-AUC [@davis2006relationship_pr_roc; @saito2015pr_more_informative_imbalanced; @leborgne2022fraud_detection_handbook]. The gap this thread leaves is methodological placement. Resampling and reweighting both presuppose a model that is *trained* on the rebalanced data or objective; an ICL FTM is frozen and cannot be retrained per objective. RAP can be read as relocating SMOTE-style oversampling and cost-sensitive intent from training time into test-time context construction, but it differs in that the oversampling duplicates real fraud rows with replacement rather than synthesizing interpolated ones, and it couples that rebalancing with relevance-based retrieval — a combination the classical imbalance literature does not address for frozen ICL models.

## Retrieval-augmented and context-selection for in-context learning

The fourth thread is the one RAP most directly extends. RAP retrieves a structurally similar context for each test batch using k-nearest-neighbour (kNN) retrieval in scaled feature space, then enforces a controlled fraud ratio by oversampling. The retrieval half is, by now, well established for tabular models. TabR augments a tabular deep network with a kNN-like retrieval module and matches or beats gradient-boosted trees [@gorishniy2024tabr_nearest_neighbors]; TabDPT trains retrieval directly into a tabular foundation model, retrieving a query-specific context at both training and inference time [@ma2024tabdpt]; and LoCalPFN retrieves a local kNN neighbourhood for TabPFN and then fine-tunes the model on it [@thomas2024localpfn_retrieval_finetuning]. Crucially, LoCalPFN's frozen, retrieval-only variant (its "TabPFN-kNN" ablation) is *exactly* a frozen kNN context for TabPFN, and it already shows retrieval beating a random context — so neither retrieval-augmented tabular ICL nor its frozen, test-time form is novel to this thesis. The closest work on the imbalance axis, AWARE, *learns* a task-aligned retrieval embedding for tabular ICL and reports that naive distance-based retrieval degrades under severe class imbalance because neighbourhoods skew to the majority class [@pham2026aware]; but it trains that embedding per dataset, targets clinical electronic-health records rather than fraud, and never controls the in-context class ratio. What is absent from all of this work is deliberate control of the *label composition* of the retrieved context — the lever RAP adds. Within the broader FTM literature, the robustness study cited above is the nearest precedent for treating the in-context set as a controllable input [@djilani2025robustness_tabular_foundation_models], and TabPFN Unleashed touches retrieval-style context handling as a scaling device [@liu2025tabpfn_unleashed], but neither targets imbalance.

On the language-model side, the sensitivity of ICL to *which* demonstrations are supplied is well documented: retrieving semantically similar examples by kNN improves few-shot performance over random selection [@liu2022good_in_context_examples], a learned retriever improves it further [@rubin2022learning_to_retrieve_prompts], and even the *order* of the demonstrations can swing accuracy from near state-of-the-art to near chance [@lu2022fantastically_ordered_prompts; @zhao2021calibrate_before_use]. These results establish context composition as a first-class lever — the premise RAP builds on. The retrieval machinery itself is classical: nearest-neighbour classification dates to @cover1967nearest_neighbor_pattern_classification, and standardising features before computing distances, so that no single high-variance feature dominates the metric, is standard practice [@hastie2009elements_statistical_learning].

Two findings from adjacent settings make RAP's central question genuinely open rather than a foregone conclusion. On balanced tabular data, random sketching of the TabPFN context is a strong baseline that smart *global* selection (k-means, coreset) fails to beat [@feuer2023scaling_tabpfn]; and in language-model ICL, rebalancing the class ratio of the demonstration pool — the very lever RAP pulls — was found *ineffective*, with stratified 50/50 selection actually reducing accuracy [@gao2025imbalanced_annotations]. Whether per-batch retrieval and explicit ratio control overturn these results under heavy *tabular* imbalance is precisely what RAP tests; a null result would itself extend these findings to a new regime.

Two features distinguish RAP within this thread, and only the second is novel. First, retrieval — confirmatory: condition C3 reproduces the frozen kNN context already studied for TabPFN [@thomas2024localpfn_retrieval_finetuning] and re-tests it on modern FTMs under heavy imbalance. Second, and the genuine contribution, retrieval is coupled with explicit fraud-ratio control: condition C4 sweeps target ratios (5, 10, 20, 30, and 50 percent) and fills the fraud quota with replacement when unique training fraud is exhausted, so oversampling is the method rather than a fallback. The only prior method to rebalance a retrieved ICL context for imbalance, IM-Context, does so for *regression* with a fixed inverse-density mixture and no ratio sweep, on small early ICL backbones [@nejjar2024im_context]; RAP instead treats the in-context fraud ratio as a tunable quantity for binary classification on modern tabular FTMs. The design is also decomposable: C3 versus C1 isolates the relevance effect, C4 versus C3 the ratio effect, and C2 (stratified, no retrieval) gives a retrieval-free isolation of the ratio effect — an attribution prior context-scaling work does not attempt. The retrieval and ratio-control conditions (C3 and C4) are not yet implemented at the time of writing; the corresponding results are pending and reported in later chapters as part of this thesis's experiments.

## Summary of gaps

Across the four threads, the niche is precise. Retrieval-augmented tabular ICL is established — including its frozen, test-time form (LoCalPFN's TabPFN-kNN) [@thomas2024localpfn_retrieval_finetuning; @ma2024tabdpt] — and a learned-retrieval method has begun to address imbalance, but in the clinical domain and via per-dataset training [@pham2026aware]. What no work does is treat the in-context *label ratio* as a controlled, swept lever for frozen off-the-shelf tabular FTMs under heavy class imbalance; and the two most relevant adjacent results point in opposite directions — random selection is hard to beat [@feuer2023scaling_tabpfn], yet ICL ratio-rebalancing can fail [@gao2025imbalanced_annotations]. Resolving whether controlled fraud-ratio context construction helps frozen tabular FTMs on fraud — and decomposing any gain into a relevance and a ratio component — is the contribution of this thesis. The thesis is therefore deliberately positioned so that its novelty rests on the ratio-control sweep (RQ4) and the relevance/ratio decomposition, with the relevance effect (RQ3) framed as a confirmatory re-test rather than a discovery.


{{< pagebreak >}}

# Methods {#sec-methods}

This chapter specifies the experimental design for evaluating Retrieval-Augmented Prediction (RAP). Section 4.1 formalises test-time context construction for an in-context-learning (ICL) tabular foundation model (FTM) under a context budget and extreme class imbalance. Section 4.2 describes the RAP pipeline (retriever, sampler, context builder, batching). Section 4.3 defines the four experimental conditions and the decomposition that separates retrieval relevance from fraud-ratio control. Section 4.4 lists the models and the rationale for the gradient-boosted-decision-tree (GBDT) baseline protocol. Section 4.5 defines the evaluation metrics. Throughout, the implemented baseline conditions (C1, C2) are distinguished from the RAP conditions (C3, C4), whose design is fixed here but whose results are pending the Phase 3 implementation.

## Problem formulation {#sec-problem}

An ICL FTM such as TabPFN [@hollmann2025accurate_tabular_foundation_model] or TabICLv2 [@qu2026tabiclv2] makes a prediction in a single forward pass, conditioning on a set of labelled examples supplied at inference time rather than updating its weights. This is the few-shot, in-context paradigm established for large language models [@brown2020language_models_few_shot] and given a Bayesian interpretation by Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs), which approximate the posterior predictive distribution conditioned on the supplied examples [@muller2022transformers_bayesian_inference]. We make this conditioning explicit. Let a labelled training pool be $D_{\text{train}} = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^{n}$ with binary labels $y_i \in \{0, 1\}$ (1 = fraud). For a test point $x$, the FTM computes $f(x \mid C)$, where the *context* $C = (X_{\text{ctx}}, y_{\text{ctx}})$ is a subset of (or a resampling from) $D_{\text{train}}$. Because attention cost grows with the number of in-context rows [@vaswani2017attention_is_all_you_need], every FTM imposes a **context budget** $B$: a soft upper bound on the number of context rows it was pre-trained to handle (Section 4.4). When $n > B$, the practitioner must choose which rows enter $C$. That choice is the object of study.

Two properties of the fraud-detection setting make the choice consequential. First, the **prevalence** $\pi = \Pr[y = 1]$ is extreme: across the formal-grid datasets it ranges from 0.13% to 1.5% (Section 4.4). Second, $n \gg B$ on every formal dataset, so a context that respects the budget contains only a small slice of the training pool. Under the naive strategy of drawing $B$ rows uniformly at random, the expected number of fraud rows in the context is $B\pi$. For TabPFN v2 ($B = 10{,}000$) on PaySim ($\pi \approx 0.0013$) this is roughly 13 fraud examples; the remaining $\approx\!9{,}987$ rows are legitimate transactions, most of them uninformative for the decision boundary. The context window is, in effect, flooded with the majority class. RAP is a response to this: a test-time strategy that builds $C$ to be both *relevant* (structurally similar to the test point) and *label-balanced* (containing a controlled fraction of fraud), without retraining the FTM.

This places RAP within the established taxonomy of imbalance handling [@he2009learning_imbalanced_data], which spans data-level resampling [@chawla2002smote], cost-sensitive losses [@lin2017_focal_loss], and algorithm-level changes. RAP is a data-level intervention, but applied at *inference* to the in-context set rather than at *training* to a model's data — a distinction that matters for frozen FTMs, which cannot be re-fitted per objective. That the in-context set is a controllable test-time lever has been demonstrated adversarially for tabular FTMs [@djilani2025robustness_tabular_foundation_models]; RAP is a benign, imbalance-motivated instance of the same mechanism. It is also complementary to model-side advances such as continued pre-training on real data [@garg2025real_tabpfn] and general scaling of TabPFN's context handling [@liu2025tabpfn_unleashed], because it changes only what enters the context, not the model.

## The RAP pipeline {#sec-rap-pipeline}

RAP constructs the context per test batch from three components: a retriever, a sampler, and a context builder. Algorithm 1 gives the full per-batch procedure (from the experiment plan, §5).

```text
Inputs:  X_train, y_train            (full training pool, unscaled)
         X_test                      (test set to be scored)
         B                           (FTM context budget)
         k                           (retrieval pool size)
         r                           (target fraud ratio; None for C3)
         metric                      (cosine or euclidean)
Setup (once per split):
    scaler   <- StandardScaler().fit(X_train)          # fit on TRAIN only
    Xs_train <- scaler.transform(X_train)
    index    <- NearestNeighbors(metric).fit(Xs_train) # built ONCE
    F_global <- {i : y_train[i] == 1}                  # global fraud pool
Per-batch inference:
    batches  <- cluster_then_chunk(scaler.transform(X_test), B)  # homogeneous
    for batch in batches:
        c        <- mean(scaler.transform(batch))      # batch centroid (scaled)
        cand     <- index.query(c, k)                  # k nearest TRAIN indices
        if r is None:                                  # C3: keep natural ratio
            idx  <- cand
            guard_against_single_class(idx, y_train, F_global)
        else:                                          # C4: enforce ratio r
            n_fraud  <- round(r * B)
            fraud    <- fraud rows in cand
            if |fraud| < n_fraud:                      # supplement / oversample
                fraud <- fraud + sample(F_global, n_fraud - |fraud|,
                                        with_replacement = (n_fraud > |F_global|))
            legit    <- sample(legit rows in cand, B - n_fraud)
            idx      <- shuffle(fraud[:n_fraud] + legit)
        X_ctx, y_ctx <- X_train[idx], y_train[idx]     # UNSCALED rows
        model.fit(X_ctx, y_ctx)
        probs[batch] <- model.predict_proba(batch)[:, 1]
```

**Retriever.** Retrieval operates in a `StandardScaler` feature space fit on the training pool only (no test leakage), so that Euclidean and cosine distances are not dominated by high-variance columns. A `NearestNeighbors` index is built once per dataset–seed split and reused across every batch and condition; this amortises the dominant index-construction cost. Each test batch is reduced to its centroid in scaled space, and the top-$k$ nearest training rows are retrieved. The retrieval metric (cosine versus Euclidean) is a configurable factor to be resolved on the development dataset in Phase 3. A standing caveat applies to BankSim: its `customer` and `merchant` features are ordinal-encoded entity identifiers, and distances over an arbitrary integer coding of identities carry no geometric meaning, so retrieval relevance is expected to be weak for that dataset and will be flagged in the results.

**Scaling is for the index only.** The scaled features serve solely to define neighbourhoods; the context rows passed to the FTM are the original **unscaled** values. FTMs ingest raw features under all conditions, matching the C1/C2 baselines and avoiding a confound between scaling and retrieval.

**Sampler.** Under C4, the sampler enforces a target fraud ratio $r$ in the context. It first takes the fraud rows present in the retrieved candidate pool; if these are insufficient to fill the quota $\mathrm{round}(rB)$, it supplements from the global training fraud pool, and when the unique global fraud is itself exhausted it draws **with replacement**, duplicating fraud rows. This with-replacement policy is deliberate: oversampling *is* the method, and capping the quota at the available unique fraud would silently record a target ratio that the context does not actually realise. The policy is applied uniformly across all datasets; duplication-heavy cells are annotated or excluded at analysis time using a stated duplication threshold, not removed from the grid. To make duplication auditable, every run logs both `context_fraud_n` (the number of fraud *slots* in the context) and `context_fraud_unique` (the number of *distinct* fraud rows); their ratio is the per-run duplication factor. This is analogous in spirit to classical minority oversampling [@chawla2002smote], but RAP duplicates existing fraud rows rather than synthesising interpolated ones, keeping every context row a genuine transaction.

**Context builder and batching.** The builder dispatches on the condition and returns $(X_{\text{ctx}}, y_{\text{ctx}})$ of length $\min(n, B)$. For the retrieval conditions, the test set is partitioned into homogeneous batches before scoring: test rows are clustered in scaled space (e.g. mini-batch k-means, or sorting by the first principal component) and grouped, so that each batch centroid is representative of its members and the retrieved context is genuinely relevant to them. For the non-retrieval baselines (C1, C2) the context is fixed, so test rows are independent given $C$ and batching is purely a memory device with no effect on results.

## Experimental conditions {#sec-conditions}

Four context-construction conditions are evaluated. C1 and C2 are implemented; C3 and C4 are specified here and implemented in Phase 3 (`src/rap/` currently exposes only its package init, and the runner raises `NotImplementedError` for these conditions).

**C1 — Random (baseline).** If $n \le B$ the whole training pool is used; otherwise $B$ rows are drawn uniformly at random *without replacement*. The natural fraud ratio is preserved. The context is built once and reused for all test rows.

**C2 — Stratified 50:50.** The context targets $\lfloor B/2 \rfloor$ fraud rows and the remainder legitimate, sampled without replacement. When unique training fraud is scarcer than the target, the fallback takes *all* fraud rows and fills the rest with legitimate ones; C2 is therefore "as close to 50:50 as the available fraud allows," not a guaranteed even split. C2 isolates the effect of the context fraud *ratio* relative to C1, holding the (random) relevance fixed.

**C3 — kNN, natural ratio (control).** Retrieval as in Algorithm 1 with $r$ unset: the context keeps whatever fraud ratio the retrieved neighbourhood happens to contain. A guard is required because a fraud-free retrieved context yields a single-class $y_{\text{ctx}}$, which breaks `predict_proba(...)[:, 1]`; the guard supplements at least one fraud (and one legitimate) row so both classes are present.

**C4 — kNN + ratio (full RAP).** Retrieval as in C3, followed by the sampler enforcing a target fraud ratio swept over $\{0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.50\}$.

**Decomposition.** The conditions form an additive ladder C1 → C3 → C4 that separates two effects. C3 versus C1 isolates the **relevance** effect — the benefit of retrieving a structurally similar context, holding the fraud ratio at its natural value. C4 versus C3 isolates the **ratio** effect — the additional benefit of fraud-ratio tuning, holding retrieval fixed. C2 versus C1 provides a complementary, retrieval-free isolation of the ratio effect. This maps onto the research questions: RQ1 compares FTMs to GBDTs under random subsampling (C1); RQ2 asks whether random subsampling degrades as datasets grow (C1 across size tiers); RQ3 asks whether retrieval improves over random subsampling (C3 versus C1); RQ4 seeks the optimal context fraud ratio (the C4 sweep). Because C3 coincides with the frozen kNN-context baseline already demonstrated for TabPFN [@thomas2024localpfn_retrieval_finetuning; @ma2024tabdpt], RQ3 is largely confirmatory; the C4 ratio sweep (RQ4) is the design's primary, novel element. GBDT baselines run under C1 only (see Section 4.4).

## Models {#sec-models}

**Tabular foundation models.** Five FTMs are targeted, all run on GPU (`device="cuda"`). Four are members of the TabPFN family [@hollmann2025accurate_tabular_foundation_model; @grinsztajn2025tabpfn25_arxiv] and one is the alternative TabICLv2 architecture [@qu2026tabiclv2], included to test whether RAP's benefits generalise beyond TabPFN. @tbl-ftms lists their context budgets, taken from the model wrappers (`CONTEXT_LIMITS`). The runner uses 100% of each budget: `context_size = min(n_train, B)`. Budgets are soft (the pre-training range), not hard caps; the larger 50k-row budgets directly affect C4 feasibility, since at those sizes no formal dataset reaches a fraud ratio of 20% or more without with-replacement oversampling, and the smallest dataset, EU-CC, reaches no swept ratio on any model without it.

| Model key | Model | Context budget (rows × features) | License |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tabpfn_v2` | TabPFN v2 | 10,000 × 500 | ungated |
| `tabpfn_25` | TabPFN 2.5 | 50,000 × 2,000 | gated (accepted) |
| `tabpfn_26` | TabPFN 2.6 | 50,000 × 2,000 | gated (accepted) |
| `tabpfn_3` | TabPFN v3 | 50,000 × 2,000 (provisional) | gated (acceptance pending) |
| `tabiclv2` | TabICLv2 | 48,000 × 500 | BSD-3 |

: Tabular foundation models and their context budgets. TabPFN versions are loaded through `tabpfn` 8.0.8; TabICLv2 through `tabicl`. Library versions are recorded per run for provenance. {#tbl-ftms}

TabPFN versions are resolved through `TabPFNClassifier.create_default_for_version(...)`, with weights lazy-loaded on first fit and reused thereafter so that one-time setup cost is timed separately from context fitting. TabPFN v3 requires a one-time license acceptance for the token-holding account; until that is granted it is excluded from the grid driver and has no results, so the in-flight grid is effectively four FTMs. Its 50k-row context is the operational budget configured in this thesis's wrapper, comfortably within TabPFN v3's architectural capacity — the v3 technical report scales in-context learning to roughly one million training rows [@grinsztajn2026tabpfn3_technical_report].

Each FTM prediction averages over `n_estimators` ensemble passes, a deep-ensemble-style averaging that improves stability [@lakshminarayanan2017deep_ensembles]. The library default is 8, but **all reported FTM grid results use `n_estimators = 4`**, a settled decision for tractability on a single GPU (the grid driver sets it for every FTM run). Reducing the count speeds prediction roughly linearly but changes outputs, and the count is part of the configuration hash; consequently, single ad-hoc runs that omit the flag use the default of 8 and are *not* comparable to grid results — the `n_estimators` column must be checked before any comparison.

**GBDT baselines.** Two gradient-boosted-decision-tree models serve as strong reference baselines, reflecting the long-standing dominance of tree ensembles on tabular data [@grinsztajn2022why_tree_based]: XGBoost [@chen2016xgboost_scalable_tree_boosting] and CatBoost [@dorogush2018catboost], the latter chosen partly for its native categorical handling given the categorical features in several fraud datasets. Both use 2,000 boosting rounds at depth 6, learning rate 0.05, and subsample 0.8; both auto-set `scale_pos_weight = n_neg / max(n_pos, 1)` to counter imbalance, hold out a stratified 10% of training data for early stopping with patience 50, and use a precision-recall objective for the stopping metric (`aucpr` / `PRAUC`).

**Why GBDTs run under C1 only, on the full training set.** The GBDTs are trained on the *entire* training pool with no context limit, and only under C1. This is deliberate, not an oversight: the limited context window is an *inherent property of the FTM architecture* that the thesis sets out to evaluate, not a constraint to impose on every model. The FTM-versus-GBDT comparison therefore measures how an FTM operating under its architectural budget fares against a model that sees all available data — the central tension of whether context-aware ICL can close the gap to GBDTs under heavy imbalance. Applying a context budget to the GBDTs would handicap them artificially and obscure that comparison.

## Evaluation metrics {#sec-metrics}

All metrics are computed from the predicted positive-class probabilities of the scored test set. Under heavy imbalance, accuracy and threshold-dependent measures are misleading, so the protocol follows established ROC/precision-recall practice for skewed problems [@fawcett2006roc_analysis]. When the scored test set contains fewer than two classes, all metrics are returned as not-a-number by a guard. Five metrics are reported per run; the first three are primary.

**PR-AUC (primary), prevalence-corrected.** The area under the precision–recall curve (average precision) is the headline metric: it tracks performance on the minority class and is far more informative than ROC-AUC under extreme imbalance [@davis2006relationship_pr_roc; @saito2015pr_more_informative_imbalanced]. A subtlety arises from test-set negative subsampling (Section 4.4 of the data chapter): to bound prediction cost, large datasets keep *all* positives but downsample negatives to a per-dataset cap (30,000; EU-CC is exempt and scored in full). Subsampling negatives inflates the empirical positive-to-negative ratio and hence empirical precision. Because ROC counts (TPR, FPR) are invariant to random negative subsampling, precision is recomputed at the true full-split prevalence $\pi$,
$$\text{precision}(t) = \frac{\pi \cdot \text{TPR}(t)}{\pi \cdot \text{TPR}(t) + (1-\pi)\,\text{FPR}(t)},$$
and integrated as $\text{AP} = \sum_k (\text{recall}_k - \text{recall}_{k-1})\,\text{precision}_k$ over score-sorted thresholds (`ap_at_prevalence`). At $\pi$ equal to the observed prevalence this equals scikit-learn's `average_precision_score` to machine precision, so unsubsampled datasets (EU-CC) are unaffected. This correction is what allows the dominant runtime speedup from negative subsampling without biasing the primary metric.

**Recall@1%FPR and Recall@5%FPR (primary), conservative step values.** Fraud systems operate at fixed, low false-positive budgets, so recall at 1% and 5% FPR are reported [@leborgne2022fraud_detection_handbook; @mcclish1989partial_roc_curve]. Each is the **highest TPR among operating points with FPR $\le$ target** on the empirical ROC curve — a conservative step-function read, not a linear interpolation. Interpolation is deliberately avoided: an interpolated (FPR, TPR) pair between two ROC vertices does not correspond to any achievable decision threshold, so interpolating *overestimates* recall, markedly so when the positive class is tiny and the curve is coarse (e.g. EU-CC, with roughly 100 test frauds). The step value is the highest recall attainable at a real threshold that meets the FPR budget. Recall@FPR is invariant to negative subsampling; the discrete ROC grid imparts a small downward bias of order $1/N_{\text{neg,scored}}$, negligible at $N \approx 30{,}000$.

**ROC-AUC and F1 (secondary).** ROC-AUC (invariant to negative subsampling) is reported for comparability with prior fraud-detection work. F1 is computed at a fixed 0.5 probability threshold; because that threshold is sensitive to calibration and prevalence and is not prevalence-corrected, F1 is interpreted only as a coarse secondary indicator.

**Aggregation.** Results are aggregated across the three seeds (42, 123, 7) as mean ± standard deviation, except FiFAR, which uses a fixed published split and runs at a single seed (a point estimate with no spread). Only runs at the current pipeline version are analysed.

**Status of RAP results.** The C1 and C2 conditions are fully implemented and produce the baseline tables. The C3 and C4 conditions — the relevance effect and the fraud-ratio sweep that constitute RAP's empirical contribution — are designed above but not yet implemented; their results, including the C3 single-class guard and the C4 duplication accounting, are pending Phase 3.
