# Experimental Setup

This chapter specifies the experimental apparatus in enough detail to reproduce it: the datasets and their provenance, the splitting protocol, the preprocessing steps, the software implementation and reproducibility controls, the compute environment, and the full experiment grid. Every fact stated here is grounded in the code that produced the results — the dataset registry (`src/data/schema.py`), the splitter (`src/data/splitter.py`), the model wrappers (`src/models/`), and the experiment runner (`src/experiment/runner.py`). Where a design choice has a methodological consequence (for example, retaining time columns as features, or correcting precision–recall area under the curve for negative subsampling), the choice is stated explicitly so that downstream results can be interpreted correctly.

## Datasets {#sec-datasets}

The evaluation uses six fraud-detection datasets in the formal grid plus one development-only dataset. All seven are ingested into a single DuckDB database and described by a central registry; the registry records, per dataset, the label column, the categorical features, the columns to drop (entity identifiers and temporal keys), and the split protocol. Table 1 summarises the datasets. Counts are taken from the registry and the project fact sheet.

| Dataset | Rows | Features | Fraud % | Train fraud (~) | In formal grid? | Seeds |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| eu_cc | 285k | 30 | 0.17% | 394 | Yes | 42, 123, 7 |
| cc_2025 | 500k | 11 | 1.5% | — | Yes (degenerate) | 42, 123, 7 |
| banksim | 595k | 7 | 1.2% | 5,760 | Yes (grouped split) | 42, 123, 7 |
| paysim | 6.3M | 7 | 0.13% | 6,570 | Yes | 42, 123, 7 |
| fifar | 603k | 29 | 1.2% | 5,705 | Yes (fixed split) | 1 |
| baf | 1M | 30 | 1.1% | 8,823 | Yes | 42, 123, 7 |
| ai_banking | 10k | 6 | 28.4% | — | No (dev only) | — |

: Datasets used in the thesis. "Train fraud (~)" is the approximate number of fraudulent rows in the training split, which bounds context-construction feasibility under the balanced and oversampled conditions. {#tbl-datasets}

The formal-grid datasets span a wide range of scale (285k to 6.3M rows) and feature dimensionality (7 to 30 features), but share the defining property of this thesis: heavy class imbalance, with fraud prevalence between roughly 0.13% and 1.5%. They divide cleanly by provenance. The European credit-card transactions benchmark (`eu_cc`) is the real, anonymised dataset released by the Machine Learning Group at the Université Libre de Bruxelles; its 28 features are principal components (V1–V28) of the original transaction attributes, retained alongside `Time` and `Amount` for confidentiality [@dalpozzolo2015calibrating]. It is the smallest and most extreme dataset, with only about 98 fraudulent transactions in the test split. BankSim (`banksim`) and PaySim (`paysim`) are agent-based simulators: BankSim is calibrated from aggregated payment data of a Spanish bank and emits labelled synthetic transactions over a six-month window [@lopezrojas2014banksim], while PaySim simulates mobile-money transfers from one month of logs of a real African service, injecting fraud into the TRANSFER and CASH_OUT transaction types [@lopezrojas2016_paysim]. FiFAR (`fifar`) and the Bank Account Fraud suite (`baf`) are realistic, large-scale bank-account-opening fraud datasets released by Feedzai. FiFAR ships with a pre-defined train/test split and synthetic analyst predictions for human–AI collaboration research, of which only the transaction-level features and the binary label are used here [@alves2023fifar_learning_to_defer]. BAF is a suite of six approximately one-million-row datasets engineered to expose imbalance, bias, and temporal distribution shift; this thesis uses the Base variant [@jesus2022baf_arxiv; @feedzai_baf_repo].

Two datasets receive special treatment. The AI Banking 2025 dataset (`ai_banking`) [@talha2025ai_powered_banking_fraud] is flagged development-only in the registry: at 28.4% fraud it is nearly balanced and therefore unsuitable as an imbalance benchmark. It is used solely for developing and validating the RAP (Retrieval-Augmented Prediction) pipeline and the metric implementations, and it is excluded from all reported results. The Credit Card Fraud 2025 dataset (`cc_2025`) [@rajak2025credit_card_fraud_2025] is retained in the grid but flagged degenerate. Inspection shows that its fraud labels are statistically independent of every feature: the distributions of `Amount`, `Distance`, `Is_International`, and the categorical attributes are identical between fraudulent and legitimate transactions. As a consequence, all models — foundation models and gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDTs) alike — score a precision–recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) approximately equal to the fraud rate (≈ 0.015) and a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) of approximately 0.50, i.e. random chance. The existing results are sufficient to document `cc_2025` in the thesis as a cautionary example of a poorly constructed synthetic benchmark; no further runs on it are queued, and its pre-existing result files are deliberately kept as that documentation.

## Splitting protocol

Unless a dataset overrides it, the protocol is a seeded, stratified 80/20 train/test split using three seeds (42, 123, 7). Stratification preserves the fraud rate in both partitions; if the minority class is too rare for stratification, the splitter falls back to an unstratified random split. Two datasets override the default. BankSim uses a **grouped** split by `customer`: BankSim's `customer` field is an entity identifier (roughly 4,112 customers across about 594k rows), and a random row-level split would place the same customer on both sides of the partition. The ordinal-encoded customer ID would then act as a memorisation key, leaking labels across the split and inflating measured performance. The grouped split (via `GroupShuffleSplit`) instead assigns each customer wholly to train or to test. Grouped splits are not label-stratified, but with thousands of groups the fraud rate stays close to the dataset rate. FiFAR uses its published, fixed pre-defined split; because the split is fixed, the seed has no effect and FiFAR is run with a single seed. This gives 16 dataset–seed units in the formal grid: five datasets at three seeds each, plus FiFAR at one seed.

Two methodological choices deserve emphasis. First, **time columns are deliberately kept as features** under the random split: `Time` in `eu_cc` and `step` in `banksim` and `paysim` are retained rather than dropped. This is a conscious decision — a random split can leak temporal structure between train and test — and the thesis treats the temporal-generalisation question separately as an ablation study rather than confounding it into the main grid. The natural vehicle for that ablation is BAF, whose published protocol splits by `month` (already excluded as a feature), giving a clean temporal-shift evaluation [@jesus2022baf_arxiv].

Second, **test-set negative subsampling** is applied to the large datasets to make the grid tractable. For `banksim`, `paysim`, `fifar`, and `baf`, every positive (fraudulent) test row is kept, and the negatives are randomly downsampled to a per-dataset cap of 30,000 (the registry's `test_neg_cap`). The subsample is deterministic, drawn from an independent random stream (seed XOR `0x5CA1E`) so it does not perturb the train-context sampling. `eu_cc` is always scored on the **full** test set (`test_neg_cap = None`), because with only ~98 test frauds, rare-event metrics under subsampling would be indefensible. This subsampling inflates the empirical positive-to-negative ratio and therefore empirical precision, so PR-AUC is **prevalence-corrected**: precision is recomputed at the true full-split fraud prevalence π using the relation precision(t) = π·TPR(t) / (π·TPR(t) + (1−π)·FPR(t)), and the average precision is integrated over the score-sorted thresholds. Because the true positive rate (TPR) and false positive rate (FPR) of the empirical ROC curve are invariant to random negative subsampling, this correction recovers the PR-AUC that would have been observed on the full test set; at the observed prevalence it equals the standard average precision to machine precision. Recall-at-fixed-FPR and ROC-AUC are themselves invariant to negative subsampling and need no correction. The full-split counts (true prevalence) and the actually scored counts are both recorded per run so the correction is auditable. The metric details are developed in the evaluation chapter; the relevant point here is that subsampling is the dominant predict-time speedup (roughly 42× on PaySim) while leaving the reported metrics unbiased.

## Preprocessing

The loader returns features as unscaled `float32` arrays and labels as `int32` 0/1 values. Categorical features (for example `type` in PaySim, or `payment_type` and `device_os` in BAF and FiFAR) are ordinal-encoded; unseen categories at test time map to a sentinel value of −1. Column names are lowercased and stripped, and the registry's `drop` list removes entity identifiers and temporal keys (transaction IDs, customer/merchant names, and similar) that would otherwise leak. For FiFAR, additional analyst-prediction and testbed-metadata columns are dropped by name pattern, since these encode information unavailable at prediction time.

No scaling is applied for the GBDT baselines or for the random and stratified context-construction conditions, which are scale-invariant. Feature scaling is required only for the kNN (k-nearest-neighbours) retrieval index used by the retrieval-based conditions: there, a `StandardScaler` is fit on the training split only and applied to both partitions, and the scaled arrays are used **solely** to build the retrieval index. The context rows ultimately passed to the foundation models remain unscaled. One caveat applies to BankSim: its `customer` and `merchant` categoricals are ordinal-encoded entity IDs, over which Euclidean or cosine distance is meaningless, so retrieval relevance on BankSim should be interpreted with care. The retrieval-based conditions are not yet implemented (see §5.6).

## Implementation and reproducibility

The entire training, inference, and pipeline code is written in Python and managed with the `uv` package manager, with all versions pinned in a lockfile. The foundation models come from the `tabpfn` library at version 8.0.8 — covering TabPFN v2 [@hollmann2025accurate_tabular_foundation_model], TabPFN 2.5 [@grinsztajn2025tabpfn25_arxiv; @priorlabs_tabpfn25_model_report_web], TabPFN 2.6 [@priorlabs2026tabpfn26_model_card], and TabPFN v3 [@grinsztajn2026tabpfn3_technical_report; @priorlabs2026tabpfn_release_v800] — together with TabICLv2 from the `tabicl` package [@qu2026tabiclv2]. The GBDT baselines are XGBoost [@chen2016xgboost_scalable_tree_boosting] and CatBoost [@dorogush2018catboost], described in the models chapter; both train on the **full** training set with no context limit, set `scale_pos_weight` automatically from the class counts, and use a held-out 10% validation slice for early stopping.

A single experiment run is fully specified by a configuration dictionary: dataset, model, condition, seed, and the retrieval-specific factors (batch size, retrieval pool size *k*, target fraud ratio, and retrieval metric) that apply only to the retrieval conditions, plus the foundation-model ensemble-pass count `n_estimators`. The **runner is idempotent**. It canonicalises the configuration (normalising irrelevant factors to a fixed sentinel so a stray value cannot fork an otherwise-identical run), serialises it deterministically, and takes the first 12 hexadecimal characters of the SHA-256 hash as the `run_id`. Output is written to `results/runs/{run_id}.parquet`; if that file already exists, the run is skipped. The runner is therefore safe to kill and restart. Crucially, the **pipeline version is part of the hashed configuration**: bumping it (currently version 4) invalidates all cached results, which is the mechanism used to force a clean rerun whenever model defaults or pipeline logic change. Library versions are recorded per run for provenance but are deliberately **not** hashed; the version-4 rerun keeps all reported results on one library version, avoiding a silent mix.

Two reproducibility caveats are worth stating up front. First, all reported foundation-model results use `n_estimators = 4` ensemble passes — a settled decision, set in the grid driver, to keep the full grid tractable on a single GPU; ensembling improves the stability of probabilistic predictions but costs predict time roughly linearly [@lakshminarayanan2017deep_ensembles]. The runner's own default for an ad-hoc single command is 8, so single runs invoked without an explicit `--n_estimators` are **not comparable** to grid results. Because `n_estimators` is in the configuration hash, the two settings produce distinct `run_id`s and distinct output rows, and the `n_estimators` column should always be checked before comparing. Second, all randomness flows through `numpy.random.default_rng(seed)`, so context sampling and the (independently seeded) test subsampling are fully reproducible.

## Compute environment

All foundation-model inference runs on a single NVIDIA RTX 5070 (12 GB) with `device="cuda"`; XGBoost defaults to CPU. The single-GPU budget drives several of the tractability compromises already noted — `n_estimators = 4`, test-set negative subsampling, and a model-aware predict-time memory chunk that streams test rows through the model in fixed-size groups. The chunk size is purely a memory-management device: because test rows are conditionally independent given the fixed context under the random and stratified conditions, chunking groups rows without changing any output. Of these compromises, the predict-time test subsampling is the dominant speedup. Because a concurrent GPU job may be in flight, runs are serialised through the idempotent driver rather than launched in parallel. Downstream analysis — results aggregation, tables, and figures — is done in R with Quarto and Typst; Python writes one Parquet row per run and R reads the result set directly, with no in-process bridge between the two languages.

## The experiment grid

The grid is organised around five foundation models (TabPFN v2, TabPFN 2.5, TabPFN 2.6, TabPFN v3, and TabICLv2), two GBDT baselines, four context-construction conditions (C1 random subsample; C2 stratified balanced subsample; C3 kNN retrieval at natural ratio; C4 kNN retrieval with controlled fraud-ratio oversampling — the full RAP method), and the 16 dataset–seed units. GBDTs run under C1 only, since they train on the full dataset and the limited context window is an inherent foundation-model property under study. Table 2 enumerates the planned grid counts.

| Block | Composition | Runs |
|---|---|---|
| FTM core | 5 models × 4 conditions × 16 units | 320 |
| GBDT core | 2 models × 1 condition (C1) × 16 units | 32 |
| C4 fraud-ratio sweep (net new) | 5 models × 4 extra ratios × 16 units | 320 |
| Batch-size sweep | 1 model × 4 batch sizes × 2 datasets × 3 seeds | 24 |

: Planned experiment-grid run counts. The C4 cell in "FTM core" is the default-ratio point of the sweep over {5, 10, 20, 30, 50}% fraud, so the sweep adds 4 extra ratios (net new runs), not 5. Cells beyond the already-collected C1/C2 runs on the degenerate `cc_2025` are dropped. {#tbl-grid}

At the time of writing the grid is being executed for the first two conditions. The retrieval-based conditions C3 and C4 — the core of the RAP contribution — are not yet implemented (the `src/rap/` package is a stub and the runner raises an error for those conditions), so all retrieval-effect and fraud-ratio-sweep results are pending. The TabPFN v3 weights additionally require a one-time license acceptance before they can be run; until that is in place the in-flight grid is effectively four foundation models, and the v3 cells are filled by a later idempotent rerun. Both gaps are confined to clearly demarcated blocks of Table 2.

# Results, Discussion and Conclusion

This chapter reports the empirical results of the thesis, discusses their interpretation, and concludes with limitations and future work. Because the experimental grid is still being collected at the time of writing, the chapter is organised so that the analysis plan — what each table and figure will show, how results are aggregated, and which research question (RQ) each addresses — is fully specified now, with numeric cells left as clearly-labelled placeholders to be filled as runs complete.

## Status of the experimental grid

The grid is partially collected. All results reported in the thesis are filtered to pipeline version 4 (the constant `_PIPELINE_VERSION = 4` in the run orchestrator), under which the test set is negative-subsampled on large datasets — all positives are kept, negatives are capped at 30,000 per dataset — and precision-recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) is prevalence-corrected so that it reflects the true population fraud rate rather than the inflated positive-to-negative ratio of the scored subset. Earlier pipeline-v2 and -v3 parquet files are stale and excluded from analysis, with the sole exception of the degenerate `cc_2025` dataset (discussed in §Discussion), whose pre-v4 files are retained deliberately as documentation.

Two facts about the current state must be stated plainly so that the results below are not over-read:

1. **Only the random-subsampling baseline (condition C1) and the stratified 50/50 baseline (condition C2) have been collected under pipeline v4, and only on a subset of datasets.** As of writing, v4 runs exist for BankSim (most cells), EU credit-card (EU-CC), and FiFAR, with PaySim and BAF reruns still queued. The headline comparison datasets are therefore not yet complete.
2. **The retrieval arms — C3 (k-nearest-neighbour, kNN, retrieval at the natural fraud ratio) and C4 (kNN retrieval plus fraud-ratio oversampling, i.e. Retrieval-Augmented Prediction, RAP) — are not yet implemented.** The `src/rap/` package currently contains only a stub, and the runner raises `NotImplementedError` for these conditions. **All RAP-specific results — the relevance effect (C3 versus C1) and the fraud-ratio sweep (C4) — are therefore pending, and no headline RAP numbers are available in this draft.**

Consequently this chapter presents the C1/C2 baseline analysis plan with placeholders for the still-incomplete cells, and the C3/C4 analyses entirely as a pre-registered plan. This separation is deliberate: stating the analysis design before the RAP results are in fixes the comparisons and aggregations in advance and guards against post-hoc metric selection, which is especially important under heavy class imbalance where metric choice can flatter a method [@fawcett2006roc_analysis].

Aggregation conventions, applied uniformly across all tables and figures below: each cell is the mean ± standard deviation over the dataset's seeds (42, 123, 7). FiFAR is reported as a single point with no error bar, because it uses a fixed published train/test split and is run once; this is noted wherever FiFAR appears. The primary metrics are PR-AUC (prevalence-corrected on subsampled datasets), Recall at 1% false-positive rate (FPR) and Recall at 5% FPR; ROC-AUC and F1 are secondary. Recall@FPR uses the conservative step value of the empirical ROC curve — the highest true-positive rate attainable at a real decision threshold whose FPR does not exceed the budget — rather than ROC interpolation, which would overestimate achievable recall on the coarse ROC curves produced by datasets with very few positives such as EU-CC.

## RQ1 — FTMs versus GBDTs under random subsampling (C1)

RQ1 asks whether in-context-learning (ICL) tabular foundation models (FTMs), restricted to their context window and fed a random subsample of the training data, can match gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDTs) trained on the full training set. This is the central baseline comparison: the GBDTs (XGBoost and CatBoost) are deliberately given no context limit, because the limited context window is an inherent property of ICL FTMs and is the very constraint the thesis interrogates [@grinsztajn2022why_tree_based; @chen2016xgboost_scalable_tree_boosting; @dorogush2018catboost]. The FTMs evaluated are TabPFN v2, TabPFN 2.5, TabPFN 2.6, TabPFN v3, and TabICLv2 [@hollmann2025accurate_tabular_foundation_model; @grinsztajn2025tabpfn25_arxiv; @qu2026tabiclv2]. TabPFN v3 is currently excluded from the live grid pending one-time license acceptance, so the grid in flight is effectively four FTMs plus two GBDTs.

The main RQ1 table reports, for every model × dataset cell, PR-AUC and Recall@1%FPR as mean ± sd over seeds (FiFAR single point).

> *[Placeholder: Table 1 — RQ1 main C1 comparison. Rows: XGBoost, CatBoost, TabPFN v2, TabPFN 2.5, TabPFN 2.6, TabPFN v3, TabICLv2. Columns grouped by dataset (EU-CC, BankSim, PaySim, FiFAR, BAF); two metrics per dataset (PR-AUC, Recall@1%FPR), each mean±sd over 3 seeds (FiFAR: single value). Pending grid completion (C1; PaySim/BAF reruns and TabPFN v3 cells outstanding).]*

The expected reading of this table is conditional. Prior work shows FTMs matching or beating tuned GBDTs on small and medium balanced tables [@hollmann2025accurate_tabular_foundation_model], but those benchmarks are not heavily imbalanced and the FTMs there see the whole (small) dataset. Here, on datasets with hundreds of thousands to millions of rows and fraud rates near 0.1–1.2%, a random context subsample to 10,000 rows (TabPFN v2) or ~48–50,000 rows (the larger-context models) will contain only a handful of fraud examples — at EU-CC's 0.17% rate, a 10,000-row context contains roughly 17 frauds in expectation. The plausible outcome is that GBDTs, which use all training fraud, retain an advantage on PR-AUC, and that the gap widens with dataset size and rarity. RQ1 establishes the size of that gap; the RAP arms (RQ3/RQ4) test whether retrieval can close it.

## RQ2 — does random subsampling degrade at scale? (C1 across size tiers)

RQ2 isolates the scaling behaviour of the C1 baseline. Holding the random-subsampling strategy fixed, it asks whether FTM performance degrades, relative to the full-data GBDTs, as the dataset grows and the fraction of training fraud captured by a fixed-size random context shrinks. This is the mechanism that motivates RAP: under heavy imbalance, a larger pool means a random context window is flooded with ever more irrelevant legitimate transactions. The degradation of a fixed random context as data grows has been reported for TabPFN [@thomas2024localpfn_retrieval_finetuning; @ma2024tabdpt]; RQ2 re-confirms it for the modern FTM line specifically under fraud-scale imbalance and with prevalence-corrected PR-AUC.

> *[Placeholder: Figure 1 — RQ2 C1 PR-AUC versus log10(dataset rows). One line per FTM and one per GBDT (mean over seeds, shaded ±sd band; FiFAR single marker). x-axis: log dataset size (EU-CC ≈ 285k, BankSim ≈ 595k, FiFAR ≈ 603k, BAF ≈ 1M, PaySim ≈ 6.3M). Expected: GBDT lines roughly flat or rising; FTM lines flat-to-declining, widening the GBDT–FTM gap at the high end. Pending grid completion.]*

The figure plots PR-AUC against the base-10 logarithm of dataset row count, with one trace per model. If random subsampling degrades at scale, the FTM traces should fall, or at least fail to track the GBDT traces, as size increases — most visibly between BAF (~1M rows) and PaySim (~6.3M rows). A flat GBDT trace would confirm that the effect is a context-window artefact of the FTMs rather than an intrinsic difficulty of the larger datasets. Dataset size is a coarse proxy here; the operative variable is the expected number of fraud examples surviving in a fixed-size random context, which the discussion will report alongside the figure.

## RQ3 — does retrieval improve over random subsampling? (C1 → C3 → C4 ablation)

RQ3 asks whether building the context by retrieval, rather than by random subsampling, improves detection under heavy imbalance. It is largely *confirmatory*: LoCalPFN's frozen TabPFN-kNN and TabDPT already show retrieval beating a random context for tabular ICL [@thomas2024localpfn_retrieval_finetuning; @ma2024tabdpt], so RQ3 re-tests that benefit on modern FTMs under fraud-scale imbalance — and against the competing evidence that random context selection is a strong baseline [@feuer2023scaling_tabpfn]. The thesis's novel question is RQ4. The design decomposes the answer into two interpretable effects via the C1 → C3 → C4 chain:

- **C3 versus C1 isolates the relevance effect.** C3 retrieves, for each test batch, the top-*k* nearest training rows in StandardScaler-scaled feature space (scaler fit on train only; context rows themselves remain unscaled when passed to the FTM) and keeps the *natural* fraud ratio of that neighbourhood. Any improvement over C1 is attributable to relevance alone — a structurally similar context — with the ratio held fixed.
- **C4 versus C3 isolates the ratio effect.** C4 takes the same retrieval and then enforces a target fraud ratio swept over {5%, 10%, 20%, 30%, 50%}, oversampling fraud as needed. Improvement of the best C4 ratio over C3 is attributable to ratio tuning, with retrieval held fixed.

This decomposition is the interpretive contribution of the design: it separates *which rows* are in the context (relevance) from *how balanced* the context is (ratio), two confounded levers in any single rebalanced-context method. Framing the in-context set as a controllable test-time lever follows the FTM-robustness literature, which manipulates the context adversarially [@djilani2025robustness_tabular_foundation_models]; RAP is a benign, imbalance-motivated instance of the same mechanism. Conceptually, RAP rebalances at inference time what SMOTE and focal loss rebalance at training time [@chawla2002smote; @lin2017_focal_loss; @he2009learning_imbalanced_data], with the advantage that it requires no retraining of the frozen FTM. The only prior method to combine retrieval with imbalance handling for tabular ICL, AWARE, does so by *learning* a task-aligned retrieval embedding rather than by controlling the context ratio [@pham2026aware]; RAP keeps both the model and the retriever fixed and intervenes only on the label composition.

> *[Placeholder: Table 2 / Figure 2 — RQ3 ablation per dataset. Per dataset and FTM, four bars or columns: C1 (random), C2 (stratified 50/50), C3 (kNN, natural ratio), C4-best (kNN + best swept fraud ratio). Metric: PR-AUC mean±sd over seeds (FiFAR single point). Annotate the C3−C1 gap (relevance) and the C4best−C3 gap (ratio). Pending C3/C4 implementation (Phase 3).]*

C2 (stratified 50/50 over the whole training set, no retrieval) is included in this comparison as a second baseline: it rebalances the ratio without relevance, so the contrast C2-versus-C4 indirectly cross-checks whether retrieval adds anything beyond rebalancing. Under the imbalance hypothesis, the expected ordering is C1 < C2 ≈ C3 < C4-best, but the relative size of the relevance and ratio effects is exactly what the experiment is designed to measure and is not assumed.

A required implementation detail, noted here because it conditions the results: C3 must guard against fraud-free retrieved contexts, since a single-class context label vector breaks the positive-class probability extraction. The planned guard supplements an all-legitimate neighbourhood with fraud drawn from the global training pool.

## RQ4 — the optimal context fraud ratio (C4 sweep)

RQ4 is the thesis's primary and most novel question: what fraud ratio in the retrieved context maximises detection, and is the optimum stable across datasets and models? No retrieval-augmented tabular method controls the in-context label ratio, and the closest evidence is discouraging — in language-model ICL, rebalancing the demonstration class ratio (including a 50/50 split) was found ineffective or harmful [@gao2025imbalanced_annotations], and on balanced tabular data smart context selection barely beats random [@feuer2023scaling_tabpfn]. Whether the heavy-imbalance fraud regime behaves differently is an open question, so a null result or an interior optimum is each an informative finding. This sweep underlies the "C4-best" column of the RQ3 ablation.

> *[Placeholder: Figure 3 — RQ4 PR-AUC by context fraud ratio. x-axis: target fraud ratio {0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.50}; y-axis: PR-AUC (mean±sd over seeds; FiFAR single point). One panel per dataset, one line per FTM. Annotate cells whose duplication factor (context_fraud_n / context_fraud_unique) exceeds the stated threshold. Pending C4 implementation.]*

The natural hypothesis is an interior optimum — too little fraud reproduces the C1 problem, while a fully balanced 50/50 context over-represents fraud relative to deployment and may hurt calibration and precision — but the curve shape is an empirical question. The figure will also expose the cost of oversampling: at the larger context sizes (~48–50k) no dataset reaches the 20% ratio or above using unique fraud rows alone, so high-ratio cells are achieved by duplicating fraud examples. The duplication factor is logged per run (the ratio of fraud slots to distinct fraud rows), and cells above a stated duplication threshold are annotated or excluded at analysis time rather than silently reported.

## Discussion

**The degenerate `cc_2025` dataset.** The Credit Card Fraud 2025 synthetic dataset is retained in the thesis not as a result but as a cautionary example. Its fraud labels are statistically independent of every feature — amount, distance, international flag and so on are identically distributed for fraud and non-fraud — so no model can do better than chance. Every model scores PR-AUC ≈ 0.015 (the fraud rate) and ROC-AUC ≈ 0.50, exactly as theory predicts for label-independent features. This is a useful negative control in two ways. First, it validates the evaluation pipeline: a prevalence-corrected PR-AUC that lands on the base rate, and a ROC-AUC of 0.5, are the correct outputs for an uninformative dataset, so the metrics are behaving as intended. Second, it is a concrete warning about synthetic fraud benchmarks: a dataset can look realistic (plausible columns, plausible imbalance) while encoding no learnable signal at all. Because no further `cc_2025` runs add information, the dataset is excluded from the active grid and documented only as an example of a poorly-constructed synthetic benchmark, a concern echoed in the synthetic-data literature on realism [@altman2023realistic_synthetic_aml; @huda2025amlnet_framework].

**Library-version provenance.** Every run records the resolved `tabpfn` and `tabicl` library versions (currently `tabpfn` 8.0.8). These versions are recorded for provenance but are deliberately *not* part of the configuration hash. The risk this creates — a silent mixture of results produced by different library versions — is managed by bumping the pipeline version and rerunning the whole grid on a single library version, so that all reported v4 results share one software stack. This is a deliberate methodological choice: provenance fields make the version auditable per row, while the full-rerun discipline keeps the comparison clean.

**Interpretive value of the relevance-versus-ratio decomposition.** Most context-rebalancing or scaling approaches for TabPFN change retrieval and balance together [@liu2025tabpfn_unleashed], leaving it unclear which lever drives any gain. The C1 → C3 → C4 chain is designed so that the two effects can be read off separately. If, as expected, the experiments show that ratio tuning contributes most of the benefit, that has a practical implication: a cheaper stratified context (C2) might recover much of RAP's gain without per-batch retrieval. If instead relevance dominates, retrieval is essential and the method cannot be shortcut. Either outcome is informative, and the value of the design is that it can tell the two apart rather than reporting a single conflated number. This positions RAP as a test-time, training-free intervention complementary to model-side advances such as better priors [@garg2025real_tabpfn] and to the broader finding that, under extreme imbalance, the training objective can matter more than architecture [@sun2025extreme_imbalance_baf]. It also separates RAP from the two closest imbalance-aware retrieval methods, both of which take the opposite, training-heavy route: AWARE learns a task-aligned retrieval embedding [@pham2026aware] and IM-Context rebalances a fixed-mixture context for regression [@nejjar2024im_context], whereas RAP intervenes only on the in-context fraud ratio of a frozen model. Should the ratio sweep show no benefit, that too is a contribution: it would extend the negative ICL-rebalancing result [@gao2025imbalanced_annotations] from language to heavily imbalanced tabular data.

## Conclusion, Limitations, and Future Work

### Limitations

Several limitations bound the interpretation of the results and the method.

**With-replacement oversampling duplication.** Filling the fraud quota in C4 duplicates fraud rows when unique training fraud is exhausted. Oversampling is the method, so duplication is not capped — but duplication-heavy cells (notably EU-CC, with only ~394 training frauds, and all models at the 48–50k context for ratios ≥ 20%) carry little new information per duplicate. These cells are annotated or excluded via a stated duplication threshold at analysis time, not removed from the grid, so the protocol stays uniform across datasets while the reporting stays honest. This design also inherits a known weakness: SMOTE's original analysis found that with-replacement duplication of minority examples does not significantly improve minority-class recognition relative to feature-space interpolation [@chawla2002smote]. RAP duplicates rather than synthesises because a frozen FTM consumes real rows and cannot ingest interpolated points without an encoder, so every context row stays a genuine, audit-traceable transaction; whether duplication suffices or interpolation-style synthesis would help is left to future work.

**kNN over ordinal-encoded entity IDs.** Retrieval (C3/C4) computes distances in scaled feature space, but some categorical features are ordinal-encoded entity identifiers — most clearly BankSim's `customer` and `merchant`. Euclidean or cosine distance over an arbitrary integer ID coding is meaningless, so retrieval relevance is questionable on such datasets and is flagged accordingly. This is also why BankSim uses a grouped-by-customer split: a row-level split would let the encoded customer ID act as a label-leaking memorisation key [@lopezrojas2014banksim].

**Single-GPU scale.** The entire grid runs on one NVIDIA 5070, forcing tractability compromises: a fixed four-pass FTM ensemble, test-set negative subsampling, and predict chunking. Negative subsampling and chunking are result-neutral by construction (Recall@FPR and ROC-AUC are invariant to negative subsampling, PR-AUC is prevalence-corrected, and test rows are independent given a fixed context), but the ensemble-size choice is not.

**The `n_estimators = 4` trade-off.** All reported FTM grid results use four ensemble passes, half the library default of eight, to keep the full grid tractable on one GPU. Reducing the ensemble size speeds prediction roughly linearly but changes outputs, and it is part of the configuration hash. Single ad-hoc command-line runs default to eight passes and are therefore *not* comparable to grid runs; comparisons must always check the `n_estimators` column [@lakshminarayanan2017deep_ensembles].

**Random rather than temporal split.** The main grid uses random stratified splits and deliberately keeps time columns (`Time` in EU-CC, `step` in BankSim and PaySim) as features. This can leak temporal structure and is stated explicitly as a methods choice. The temporal-distribution-shift question is deferred to an ablation rather than baked into the main comparison [@helli2024drift_resilient_tabpfn; @kim2024temporal_gnn_financial].

### Future work

The immediate priority is to finish the grid: implement the RAP modules so that C3 and C4 run, complete the PaySim and BAF v4 reruns, and add the TabPFN v3 cells once the license is accepted. Beyond completing the planned analyses (the batch-size sweep and the C4 fraud-ratio sweep), the natural extension is the temporal-split ablation using BAF's published month-based protocol, in which `month` is already excluded as a feature, to test whether RAP's benefit survives distribution shift [@jesus2022baf_arxiv; @feedzai_baf_repo]. A further direction is comparing retrieval metrics (cosine versus Euclidean) and principled handling of entity-ID features so that retrieval is meaningful on datasets like BankSim.

### Restatement of the contribution

This thesis introduces Retrieval-Augmented Prediction, a test-time context-construction strategy for in-context-learning tabular foundation models under heavy class imbalance. Rather than randomly subsampling the training set into the FTM's limited context window — which, under fraud-rate imbalance, floods the window with irrelevant legitimate transactions — RAP retrieves a structurally similar, label-balanced context around each test batch using kNN retrieval and controlled fraud-ratio oversampling. The method is training-free and operates on a frozen FTM, and its evaluation is designed to decompose the benefit into a relevance effect and a ratio effect. The baseline grid is in progress and the RAP arms are pending implementation, but the experimental design, metrics, and analysis plan presented here fix the comparison in advance so that the headline results, once collected, answer each research question directly.
